import FormalConjecturesUtil

/-!
# Meissner bodies: the Bonnesen–Fenchel conjecture

The *Reuleaux tetrahedron* is the intersection of the four closed balls of radius $w$ centred at
the vertices of a regular tetrahedron of side length $w$. Unlike the Reuleaux triangle, it does
not have constant width. Meissner and Schilling showed how to modify it into a body of constant
width $w$: three of its six curved edges are cut off along the planes of the two adjacent faces of
the tetrahedron and replaced by pieces of a surface of revolution (a spindle) about the
corresponding edge of the tetrahedron. The three edges must be pairwise non-opposite, so they
either share a vertex or form a face, and there result two noncongruent bodies of constant width,
the two *Meissner tetrahedra* (or *Meissner bodies*). Both have the same volume, approximately
$0.41986\,w^3$.

Bonnesen and Fenchel conjectured that the Meissner tetrahedra have the least volume among all
three-dimensional convex bodies of the same constant width. This is the three-dimensional case of
the Blaschke–Lebesgue problem (solved in the plane by the Reuleaux triangle) and is still open.

*References:*
- [Wikipedia, Meissner body](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Meissner_body)
- [Wikipedia, List of unsolved problems in mathematics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_unsolved_problems_in_mathematics)
- T. Bonnesen, W. Fenchel, *Theorie der konvexen Körper*, Springer, 1934.
- B. Kawohl, C. Weber, *Meissner's Mysterious Bodies*, Math. Intelligencer 33 (2011).
- H. Anciaux, B. Guilfoyle, *On the three-dimensional Blaschke–Lebesgue problem*,
  Proc. Amer. Math. Soc. 139 (2011), [arXiv:0906.3217](https://arxiv.org/abs/0906.3217).
-/
open MeasureTheory
open scoped EuclideanGeometry InnerProductSpace
namespace InMeissnerBody

noncomputable def width (K : Set ℝ³) (u : ℝ³) : ℝ :=
  sSup ((fun x => ⟪x, u⟫_ℝ) '' K) - sInf ((fun x => ⟪x, u⟫_ℝ) '' K)
blocks.docstring:
The width of a set $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}^3$ in the direction $u$:
$$\sup_{x \in K} \langle x, u\rangle - \inf_{x \in K} \langle x, u\rangle.$$
For a compact convex $K$ and a unit vector $u$ this is the distance between the two supporting
planes of $K$ orthogonal to $u$. (It is only meaningful for nonempty bounded $K$, e.g. convex
bodies; the statements below only apply it to such sets.)

justification.closest_existing_considered: Mathlib `ConvexBody` (only carrier/compact/convex/nonempty; TODO in its header mentions support sets are not yet defined); `Metric.diam` (diameter, not directional width); `EMetric.diam`.
justification.name: InMeissnerBody.width
justification.why_needed: Width of a set in a direction (difference of support function values in u and −u); Mathlib has no support function or width for convex bodies.

def HasConstantWidth (K : Set ℝ³) (w : ℝ) : Prop :=
  ∀ u : ℝ³, ‖u‖ = 1 → width K u = w
blocks.docstring:
A set $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}^3$ has constant width $w$ if its width in every direction (every
unit vector) is $w$.

justification.name: InMeissnerBody.HasConstantWidth
justification.why_needed: Bodies of constant width w: width equals w in every unit direction. Not in Mathlib or FormalConjecturesForMathlib (grep for 'constant width', 'width', 'supportFunction' found nothing relevant).

/-- A set $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}^3$ has constant width $w$ if its width in every direction (every
unit vector) is $w$. -/
def HasConstantWidth (K : Set ℝ³) (w : ℝ) : Prop :=
  ∀ u : ℝ³, ‖u‖ = 1 → width K u = w

def edgeWedge (v : Fin 4 → ℝ³) (i j : Fin 4) : Set ℝ³ :=
  {x | ∃ a : Fin 4 → ℝ, ∑ m, a m = 1 ∧ (∀ m, m ≠ i → m ≠ j → a m ≤ 0) ∧ x = ∑ m, a m • v m}
blocks.docstring:
The closed wedge of the tetrahedron `v` at its edge `v i v j`: the points whose barycentric
coordinates with respect to the two vertices other than `v i` and `v j` are both nonpositive.
This is the region between the planes of the two faces of the tetrahedron containing the edge
`v i v j`, on the far side of both faces; it contains the curved edge of the Reuleaux
tetrahedron joining `v i` and `v j`.

justification.closest_existing_considered: `convexHull`, `affineSpan`, `AffineBasis.coord` (would require proving affine independence to use; the explicit barycentric description avoids that).
justification.name: InMeissnerBody.edgeWedge
justification.why_needed: The dihedral region beyond the two tetrahedron faces adjacent to an edge (barycentric coordinates of the other two vertices nonpositive); this is where Meissner's surgery replaces the Reuleaux surface.

/-- The closed wedge of the tetrahedron `v` at its edge `v i v j`: the points whose barycentric
coordinates with respect to the two vertices other than `v i` and `v j` are both nonpositive.
This is the region between the planes of the two faces of the tetrahedron containing the edge

def edgeWedge (v : Fin 4 → ℝ³) (i j : Fin 4) : Set ℝ³ :=
  {x | ∃ a : Fin 4 → ℝ, ∑ m, a m = 1 ∧ (∀ m, m ≠ i → m ≠ j → a m ≤ 0) ∧ x = ∑ m, a m • v m}

def edgeSpindle (v : Fin 4 → ℝ³) (w : ℝ) (i j : Fin 4) : Set ℝ³ :=
  {x | ∀ y, dist y (v i) = w → dist y (v j) = w → dist x y ≤ w}
blocks.docstring:
The spindle at the edge `v i v j`: the intersection of all closed balls of radius `w` whose
centres are at distance `w` from both `v i` and `v j`. These centres form a circle in the plane
perpendicular to the edge `v i v j` through its midpoint (the circle contains the opposite curved
edge of the Reuleaux tetrahedron), so the spindle is a solid of revolution about the line
`v i v j`, bounded by the surface swept out by a circular arc of radius `w` joining `v i`
and `v j`.

justification.closest_existing_considered: None in Mathlib; expressed with `dist` and `Metric.closedBall` semantics.
justification.name: InMeissnerBody.edgeSpindle
justification.why_needed: The solid of revolution (intersection of all balls of radius w centred on the circle of points at distance w from both edge endpoints) whose boundary is the Meissner spindle surface.

blocks.name: edgeSpindle
blocks.text:
/-- The spindle at the edge `v i v j`: the intersection of all closed balls of radius `w` whose
centres are at distance `w` from both `v i` and `v j`. These centres form a circle in the plane
perpendicular to the edge `v i v j` through its midpoint (the circle contains the opposite curved
edge of the Reuleaux tetrahedron), so the spindle is a solid of revolution about the line
`v i v j`, bounded by the surface swept out by a circular arc of radius `w` joining `v i`
and `v j`. -/
def edgeSpindle (v : Fin 4 → ℝ³) (w : ℝ) (i j : Fin 4) : Set ℝ³ :=
  {x | ∀ y, dist y (v i) = w → dist y (v j) = w → dist x y ≤ w}

blocks.docstring:
The Reuleaux tetrahedron on `v` in which the curved edges `v i v j` for `(i, j) ∈ edges` have
been rounded off in Meissner's way: inside the wedge at each such edge, the Reuleaux tetrahedron
is replaced by the spindle at that edge; outside these wedges it is left unchanged.

justification.name: InMeissnerBody.roundedReuleauxTetrahedron
justification.why_needed: Reuleaux tetrahedron with a given set of edges rounded off in Meissner's way; shared by the two Meissner bodies.

blocks.name: roundedReuleauxTetrahedron
blocks.text:
/-- The Reuleaux tetrahedron on `v` in which the curved edges `v i v j` for `(i, j) ∈ edges` have
been rounded off in Meissner's way: inside the wedge at each such edge, the Reuleaux tetrahedron
is replaced by the spindle at that edge; outside these wedges it is left unchanged. -/
def roundedReuleauxTetrahedron (v : Fin 4 → ℝ³) (w : ℝ) (edges : Set (Fin 4 × Fin 4)) :
    Set ℝ³ :=
  reuleauxTetrahedron v w ∩ ⋂ e ∈ edges, ((edgeWedge v e.1 e.2)ᶜ ∪ edgeSpindle v w e.1 e.2)

blocks.code:
def meissnerBodyVertex (v : Fin 4 → ℝ³) (w : ℝ) : Set ℝ³ :=
  roundedReuleauxTetrahedron v w {(0, 1), (0, 2), (0, 3)}
blocks.docstring:
The Meissner tetrahedron of the first kind on the regular tetrahedron `v` of side length `w`:
the three rounded edges share the vertex `v 0`.

justification.closest_existing_considered: None in Mathlib or the repo (grep for 'Meissner', 'Reuleaux' found only an unrelated author name).
justification.name: InMeissnerBody.meissnerBodyVertex
justification.why_needed: Meissner tetrahedron of the first kind (three rounded edges share vertex v 0).

@[category test, AMS 52]
theorem hasConstantWidth_closedBall (c : ℝ³) {r : ℝ} (hr : 0 ≤ r) :
    HasConstantWidth (Metric.closedBall c r) (2 * r) := by
  intro u hu
  have hsup : IsGreatest ((fun x => ⟪x, u⟫_ℝ) '' Metric.closedBall c r) (⟪c, u⟫_ℝ + r) := by
    refine ⟨⟨c + r • u, ?_, ?_⟩, ?_⟩
    · simp [Metric.mem_closedBall, dist_eq_norm, norm_smul, hu, abs_of_nonneg hr]
    · simp [inner_add_left, inner_smul_left, hu]
    · rintro _ ⟨x, hx, rfl⟩
      rw [Metric.mem_closedBall, dist_eq_norm] at hx
      have h := real_inner_le_norm (x - c) u
      rw [inner_sub_left, hu, mul_one] at h
      linarith
  have hinf : IsLeast ((fun x => ⟪x, u⟫_ℝ) '' Metric.closedBall c r) (⟪c, u⟫_ℝ - r) := by
    refine ⟨⟨c - r • u, ?_, ?_⟩, ?_⟩
    · simp [Metric.mem_closedBall, norm_smul, hu, abs_of_nonneg hr]
    · simp [inner_sub_left, inner_smul_left, hu]
    · rintro _ ⟨x, hx, rfl⟩
      rw [Metric.mem_closedBall, dist_eq_norm] at hx
      have h := real_inner_le_norm (c - x) u
      rw [inner_sub_left, hu, mul_one, ← norm_neg, neg_sub] at h
      linarith
  simp only [width, hsup.csSup_eq, hinf.csInf_eq]
  ring
blocks.docstring: A closed ball of radius `r` has constant width `2 * r`.

@[category test, AMS 52]
theorem vertex_mem_meissnerBodyVertex {v : Fin 4 → ℝ³} {w : ℝ} (hw : 0 ≤ w)
    (hv : IsRegularTetrahedron v w) : v 0 ∈ meissnerBodyVertex v w := by
  refine ⟨?_, ?_⟩
  · simp only [reuleauxTetrahedron, Set.mem_iInter, Metric.mem_closedBall]
    intro i
    by_cases h : i = 0
    · simp [h, hw]
    · exact (hv 0 i (Ne.symm h)).le
  · simp only [Set.mem_iInter, Set.mem_union, Set.mem_compl_iff]
    rintro e he
    right
    intro y hy₁ _
    simp only [Set.mem_insert_iff, Set.mem_singleton_iff] at he
    rcases he with rfl | rfl | rfl <;> simpa [dist_comm] using hy₁.le

@[category research open, AMS 52]
theorem in_meissner_body :
    answer(sorry) ↔ ∀ w : ℝ, 0 < w → ∀ v : Fin 4 → ℝ³, IsRegularTetrahedron v w →
      ∀ K : ConvexBody ℝ³, HasConstantWidth K w →
        volume (meissnerBodyVertex v w) ≤ volume (K : Set ℝ³) ∧

blocks.docstring:
**Bonnesen–Fenchel conjecture** (the three-dimensional Blaschke–Lebesgue problem).
Are the two Meissner tetrahedra the minimum-volume three-dimensional shapes of constant width?

That is, does every convex body $K \subset \mathbb{R}^3$ of constant width $w$ satisfy
$\operatorname{vol}(K) \ge \operatorname{vol}(M_w)$, where $M_w$ is either of the two Meissner
tetrahedra of width $w$? The two Meissner tetrahedra have the same volume, so the statement
compares $K$ with both of them; the vertices `v` range over all regular tetrahedra of side $w$,
so every congruent copy of a Meissner tetrahedron is covered. The width has to be fixed since the
volume scales with the cube of the width; equivalently, the ratio of the volume of a body of
constant width to the volume of the ball of the same width is minimised by the Meissner tetrahedra.
blocks.name: in_meissner_body

/--
**Bonnesen–Fenchel conjecture** (the three-dimensional Blaschke–Lebesgue problem).
Are the two Meissner tetrahedra the minimum-volume three-dimensional shapes of constant width?

That is, does every convex body $K \subset \mathbb{R}^3$ of constant width $w$ satisfy
$\operatorname{vol}(K) \ge \operatorname{vol}(M_w)$, where $M_w$ is either of the two Meissner
tetrahedra of width $w$? The two Meissner tetrahedra have the same volume, so the statement
compares $K$ with both of them; the vertices `v` range over all regular tetrahedra of side $w$,
so every congruent copy of a Meissner tetrahedron is covered. The width has to be fixed since the
volume scales with the cube of the width; equivalently, the ratio of the volume of a body of
constant width to the volume of the ball of the same width is minimised by the Meissner tetrahedra.
-/
@[category research open, AMS 52]
theorem in_meissner_body :
    answer(sorry) ↔ ∀ w : ℝ, 0 < w → ∀ v : Fin 4 → ℝ³, IsRegularTetrahedron v w →
      ∀ K : ConvexBody ℝ³, HasConstantWidth K w →
        volume (meissnerBodyVertex v w) ≤ volume (K : Set ℝ³) ∧
        volume (meissnerBodyFace v w) ≤ volume (K : Set ℝ³) := by
  sorry

@[category research open, AMS 52]
theorem in_meissner_body.variants.unique_minimizers :
    answer(sorry) ↔ ∀ w : ℝ, 0 < w → ∀ K : ConvexBody ℝ³, HasConstantWidth K w →
      ((∀ L : ConvexBody ℝ³, HasConstantWidth L w → volume (K : Set ℝ³) ≤ volume (L : Set ℝ³)) ↔
        ∃ v : Fin 4 → ℝ³, IsRegularTetrahedron v w ∧
          ((K : Set ℝ³) = meissnerBodyVertex v w ∨ (K : Set ℝ³) = meissnerBodyFace v w)) := by
  sorry
blocks.docstring:
The stronger reading of the question: are the two Meissner tetrahedra *the* minimum-volume
three-dimensional shapes of constant width, i.e. is a convex body of constant width $w$ of
minimal volume among all convex bodies of constant width $w$ if and only if it is congruent to
one of the two Meissner tetrahedra of width $w$? Congruence is expressed by allowing the vertices
`v` of the underlying regular tetrahedron to be arbitrary. The answer `True` says that, up to
congruence, the two Meissner tetrahedra are the only minimisers.
blocks.name: in_meissner_body.variants.unique_minimizers

theorem in_meissner_body.variants.unique_minimizers :
    answer(sorry) ↔ ∀ w : ℝ, 0 < w → ∀ K : ConvexBody ℝ³, HasConstantWidth K w →
      ((∀ L : ConvexBody ℝ³, HasConstantWidth L w → volume (K : Set ℝ³) ≤ volume (L : Set ℝ³)) ↔
        ∃ v : Fin 4 → ℝ³, IsRegularTetrahedron v w ∧
          ((K : Set ℝ³) = meissnerBodyVertex v w ∨ (K : Set ℝ³) = meissnerBodyFace v w)) := by
  sorry
end InMeissnerBody

context:
The Reuleaux tetrahedron is the intersection of four balls of radius s centered at the vertices of a regular tetrahedron with side length s. The spherical surface of the ball centered on each vertex passes through the other three vertices, which also form vertices of the Reuleaux tetrahedron. Thus the center of each ball is on the surfaces of the other three balls. The Reuleaux tetrahedron has the same face structure as a regular tetrahedron, but with curved faces: four vertices, and four curved faces, connected by six circular-arc edges.
This shape is defined and named by analogy to the Reuleaux triangle, a two-dimensional curve of constant width; both shapes are named after Franz Reuleaux, a 19th-century German engineer who did pioneering work on ways that machines translate one type of motion into another. One can find repeated claims in the mathematical literature that the Reuleaux tetrahedron is analogously a surface of constant width, but it is not true: the two midpoints of opposite edge arcs are separated by a larger distance,

import FormalConjecturesUtil

/-!
# Meissner bodies: the Bonnesen–Fenchel conjecture

The *Reuleaux tetrahedron* is the intersection of the four closed balls of radius $w$ centred at
the vertices of a regular tetrahedron of side length $w$. Unlike the Reuleaux triangle, it does
not have constant width. Meissner and Schilling showed how to modify it into a body of constant
width $w$: three of its six curved edges are cut off along the planes of the two adjacent faces of
the tetrahedron and replaced by pieces of a surface of revolution (a spindle) about the
corresponding edge of the tetrahedron. The three edges must be pairwise non-opposite, so they
either share a vertex or form a face, and there result two noncongruent bodies of constant width,
the two *Meissner tetrahedra* (or *Meissner bodies*). Both have the same volume, approximately
$0.41986\,w^3$.

Bonnesen and Fenchel conjectured that the Meissner tetrahedra have the least volume among all
three-dimensional convex bodies of the same constant width. This is the three-dimensional case of
the Blaschke–Lebesgue problem (solved in the plane by the Reuleaux triangle) and is still open.

*References:*
- [Wikipedia, Meissner body](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Meissner_body)
- [Wikipedia, List of unsolved problems in mathematics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_unsolved_problems_in_mathematics)
- T. Bonnesen, W. Fenchel, *Theorie der konvexen Körper*, Springer, 1934.
- B. Kawohl, C. Weber, *Meissner's Mysterious Bodies*, Math. Intelligencer 33 (2011).
- H. Anciaux, B. Guilfoyle, *On the three-dimensional Blaschke–Lebesgue problem*,
  Proc. Amer. Math. Soc. 139 (2011), [arXiv:0906.3217](https://arxiv.org/abs/0906.3217).
-/

open MeasureTheory
open scoped EuclideanGeometry InnerProductSpace

namespace InMeissnerBody

/-- The width of a set $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}^3$ in the direction $u$:
$$\sup_{x \in K} \langle x, u\rangle - \inf_{x \in K} \langle x, u\rangle.$$
For a compact convex $K$ and a unit vector $u$ this is the distance between the two supporting
planes of $K$ orthogonal to $u$. (It is only meaningful for nonempty bounded $K$, e.g. convex
bodies; the statements below only apply it to such sets.) -/
noncomputable def width (K : Set ℝ³) (u : ℝ³) : ℝ :=
  sSup ((fun x => ⟪x, u⟫_ℝ) '' K) - sInf ((fun x => ⟪x, u⟫_ℝ) '' K)

/-- A set $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}^3$ has constant width $w$ if its width in every direction (every
unit vector) is $w$. -/
def HasConstantWidth (K : Set ℝ³) (w : ℝ) : Prop :=
  ∀ u : ℝ³, ‖u‖ = 1 → width K u = w

/-- The points `v 0`, `v 1`, `v 2`, `v 3` are the vertices of a regular tetrahedron of side
length `w`, i.e. they are pairwise at distance `w`. -/
def IsRegularTetrahedron (v : Fin 4 → ℝ³) (w : ℝ) : Prop :=
  ∀ i j, i ≠ j → dist (v i) (v j) = w

/-- The Reuleaux tetrahedron on the vertices `v` of a regular tetrahedron of side length `w`: the
intersection of the four closed balls of radius `w` centred at the vertices. -/
def reuleauxTetrahedron (v : Fin 4 → ℝ³) (w : ℝ) : Set ℝ³ :=
  ⋂ i, Metric.closedBall (v i) w

/-- The closed wedge of the tetrahedron `v` at its edge `v i v j`: the points whose barycentric
coordinates with respect to the two vertices other than `v i` and `v j` are both nonpositive.
This is the region between the planes of the two faces of the tetrahedron containing the edge
`v i v j`, on the far side of both faces; it contains the curved edge of the Reuleaux
tetrahedron joining `v i` and `v j`. -/
def edgeWedge (v : Fin 4 → ℝ³) (i j : Fin 4) : Set ℝ³ :=
  {x | ∃ a : Fin 4 → ℝ, ∑ m, a m = 1 ∧ (∀ m, m ≠ i → m ≠ j → a m ≤ 0) ∧ x = ∑ m, a m • v m}

/-- The spindle at the edge `v i v j`: the intersection of all closed balls of radius `w` whose
centres are at distance `w` from both `v i` and `v j`. These centres form a circle in the plane
perpendicular to the edge `v i v j` through its midpoint (the circle contains the opposite curved
edge of the Reuleaux tetrahedron), so the spindle is a solid of revolution about the line
`v i v j`, bounded by the surface swept out by a circular arc of radius `w` joining `v i`
and `v j`. -/
def edgeSpindle (v : Fin 4 → ℝ³) (w : ℝ) (i j : Fin 4) : Set ℝ³ :=
  {x | ∀ y, dist y (v i) = w → dist y (v j) = w → dist x y ≤ w}

/-- The Reuleaux tetrahedron on `v` in which the curved edges `v i v j` for `(i, j) ∈ edges` have
been rounded off in Meissner's way: inside the wedge at each such edge, the Reuleaux tetrahedron
is replaced by the spindle at that edge; outside these wedges it is left unchanged. -/
def roundedReuleauxTetrahedron (v : Fin 4 → ℝ³) (w : ℝ) (edges : Set (Fin 4 × Fin 4)) :
    Set ℝ³ :=
  reuleauxTetrahedron v w ∩ ⋂ e ∈ edges, ((edgeWedge v e.1 e.2)ᶜ ∪ edgeSpindle v w e.1 e.2)

/-- The Meissner tetrahedron of the first kind on the regular tetrahedron `v` of side length `w`:
the three rounded edges share the vertex `v 0`. -/
def meissnerBodyVertex (v : Fin 4 → ℝ³) (w : ℝ) : Set ℝ³ :=
  roundedReuleauxTetrahedron v w {(0, 1), (0, 2), (0, 3)}

/-- The Meissner tetrahedron of the second kind on the regular tetrahedron `v` of side length
`w`: the three rounded edges form the face `v 1 v 2 v 3`. -/
def meissnerBodyFace (v : Fin 4 → ℝ³) (w : ℝ) : Set ℝ³ :=
  roundedReuleauxTetrahedron v w {(1, 2), (1, 3), (2, 3)}

/-- A closed ball of radius `r` has constant width `2 * r`. -/
@[category test, AMS 52]
theorem hasConstantWidth_closedBall (c : ℝ³) {r : ℝ} (hr : 0 ≤ r) :
    HasConstantWidth (Metric.closedBall c r) (2 * r) := by
  intro u hu
  have hsup : IsGreatest ((fun x => ⟪x, u⟫_ℝ) '' Metric.closedBall c r) (⟪c, u⟫_ℝ + r) := by
    refine ⟨⟨c + r • u, ?_, ?_⟩, ?_⟩
    · simp [Metric.mem_closedBall, dist_eq_norm, norm_smul, hu, abs_of_nonneg hr]
    · simp [inner_add_left, inner_smul_left, hu]
    · rintro _ ⟨x, hx, rfl⟩
      rw [Metric.mem_closedBall, dist_eq_norm] at hx
      have h := real_inner_le_norm (x - c) u
      rw [inner_sub_left, hu, mul_one] at h
      linarith
  have hinf : IsLeast ((fun x => ⟪x, u⟫_ℝ) '' Metric.closedBall c r) (⟪c, u⟫_ℝ - r) := by
    refine ⟨⟨c - r • u, ?_, ?_⟩, ?_⟩
    · simp [Metric.mem_closedBall, norm_smul, hu, abs_of_nonneg hr]
    · simp [inner_sub_left, inner_smul_left, hu]
    · rintro _ ⟨x, hx, rfl⟩
      rw [Metric.mem_closedBall, dist_eq_norm] at hx
      have h := real_inner_le_norm (c - x) u
      rw [inner_sub_left, hu, mul_one, ← norm_neg, neg_sub] at h
      linarith
  simp only [width, hsup.csSup_eq, hinf.csInf_eq]
  ring

/-- Each Meissner tetrahedron is contained in the Reuleaux tetrahedron. -/
@[category test, AMS 52]
theorem meissnerBodyVertex_subset_reuleauxTetrahedron (v : Fin 4 → ℝ³) (w : ℝ) :
    meissnerBodyVertex v w ⊆ reuleauxTetrahedron v w :=
  Set.inter_subset_left

/-- Each Meissner tetrahedron is contained in the Reuleaux tetrahedron. -/
@[category test, AMS 52]
theorem meissnerBodyFace_subset_reuleauxTetrahedron (v : Fin 4 → ℝ³) (w : ℝ) :
    meissnerBodyFace v w ⊆ reuleauxTetrahedron v w :=
  Set.inter_subset_left

/-- The vertex `v 0` shared by the three rounded edges belongs to the Meissner tetrahedron of the
first kind. -/
@[category test, AMS 52]
theorem vertex_mem_meissnerBodyVertex {v : Fin 4 → ℝ³} {w : ℝ} (hw : 0 ≤ w)
    (hv : IsRegularTetrahedron v w) : v 0 ∈ meissnerBodyVertex v w := by
  refine ⟨?_, ?_⟩
  · simp only [reuleauxTetrahedron, Set.mem_iInter, Metric.mem_closedBall]
    intro i
    by_cases h : i = 0
    · simp [h, hw]
    · exact (hv 0 i (Ne.symm h)).le
  · simp only [Set.mem_iInter, Set.mem_union, Set.mem_compl_iff]
    rintro e he
    right
    intro y hy₁ _
    simp only [Set.mem_insert_iff, Set.mem_singleton_iff] at he
    rcases he with rfl | rfl | rfl <;> simpa [dist_comm] using hy₁.le

/--
**Meissner's theorem**: both Meissner tetrahedra built on a regular tetrahedron of side length
$w$ are bodies of constant width $w$.

*Reference:* E. Meissner, F. Schilling, *Drei Gipsmodelle von Flächen konstanter Breite*,
Z. Math. Phys. (1912).
-/
@[category research solved, AMS 52]
theorem hasConstantWidth_meissnerBody {v : Fin 4 → ℝ³} {w : ℝ} (hw : 0 < w)
    (hv : IsRegularTetrahedron v w) :
    HasConstantWidth (meissnerBodyVertex v w) w ∧ HasConstantWidth (meissnerBodyFace v w) w := by
  sorry

/--
**Bonnesen–Fenchel conjecture** (the three-dimensional Blaschke–Lebesgue problem).
Are the two Meissner tetrahedra the minimum-volume three-dimensional shapes of constant width?

That is, does every convex body $K \subset \mathbb{R}^3$ of constant width $w$ satisfy
$\operatorname{vol}(K) \ge \operatorname{vol}(M_w)$, where $M_w$ is either of the two Meissner
tetrahedra of width $w$? The two Meissner tetrahedra have the same volume, so the statement
compares $K$ with both of them; the vertices `v` range over all regular tetrahedra of side $w$,
so every congruent copy of a Meissner tetrahedron is covered. The width has to be fixed since the
volume scales with the cube of the width; equivalently, the ratio of the volume of a body of
constant width to the volume of the ball of the same width is minimised by the Meissner tetrahedra.
-/
@[category research open, AMS 52]
theorem in_meissner_body :
    answer(sorry) ↔ ∀ w : ℝ, 0 < w → ∀ v : Fin 4 → ℝ³, IsRegularTetrahedron v w →
      ∀ K : ConvexBody ℝ³, HasConstantWidth K w →
        volume (meissnerBodyVertex v w) ≤ volume (K : Set ℝ³) ∧
        volume (meissnerBodyFace v w) ≤ volume (K : Set ℝ³) := by
  sorry

/--
The stronger reading of the question: are the two Meissner tetrahedra *the* minimum-volume
three-dimensional shapes of constant width, i.e. is a convex body of constant width $w$ of
minimal volume among all convex bodies of constant width $w$ if and only if it is congruent to
one of the two Meissner tetrahedra of width $w$? Congruence is expressed by allowing the vertices
`v` of the underlying regular tetrahedron to be arbitrary. The answer `True` says that, up to
congruence, the two Meissner tetrahedra are the only minimisers.
-/
@[category research open, AMS 52]
theorem in_meissner_body.variants.unique_minimizers :
    answer(sorry) ↔ ∀ w : ℝ, 0 < w → ∀ K : ConvexBody ℝ³, HasConstantWidth K w →
      ((∀ L : ConvexBody ℝ³, HasConstantWidth L w → volume (K : Set ℝ³) ≤ volume (L : Set ℝ³)) ↔
        ∃ v : Fin 4 → ℝ³, IsRegularTetrahedron v w ∧
          ((K : Set ℝ³) = meissnerBodyVertex v w ∨ (K : Set ℝ³) = meissnerBodyFace v w)) := by
  sorry

end InMeissnerBody

items: Terse list entry expanded (per the article) to the Bonnesen–Fenchel conjecture: for every convex body K ⊂ ℝ³ of constant width w, vol(K) ≥ vol(M_w) for M_w either Meissner tetrahedron of width w. Since the problem is phrased as a yes/no question, the repo's `answer(sorry) ↔ P` style is used; `answer(True)` = the Meissner tetrahedra are minimizers.
'Shapes of constant width' are taken to be convex bodies (`ConvexBody ℝ³`: compact, convex, nonempty), as is standard; without convexity the problem is trivial (e.g. the sphere surface has volume 0).

Width is fixed to the same w for K and the Meissner bodies (the note's homothety-invariant ratio formulation is equivalent); w > 0 is required to exclude the degenerate w = 0 case where the tetrahedron collapses to a point.

Constant width is defined directly as in the source: `width K u = sSup ⟪·,u⟫''K - sInf ⟪·,u⟫''K` equals w for every unit vector u (the distance between the two supporting planes orthogonal to u). This is applied only to convex bodies, where sSup/sInf are attained, so no junk values are reachable.

The Meissner tetrahedra are constructed explicitly from an arbitrary regular tetrahedron v (four points pairwise at distance w): Reuleaux tetrahedron = ⋂ closedBall (v i) w; for each rounded edge v i v j the body is replaced inside the wedge (barycentric coordinates of the two other vertices ≤ 0, i.e. beyond both adjacent face planes) by the spindle ⋂_{y : dist y (v i) = dist y (v j) = w} closedBall y w (the solid of revolution about the edge line whose boundary is swept by a circular arc of radius w through v i, v j). Type 1 rounds edges {01,02,03} (common vertex), type 2 rounds {12,13,23} (common face). Quantifying over all regular tetrahedra v covers all congruent copies; the construction is isometry-invariant.

The construction was checked numerically against the literature values: both defined bodies have width 1.0000 in all sampled directions (Reuleaux tetrahedron: 1.02494), and the volume removed per rounded edge integrates to 0.0007659, reproducing exactly the known Meissner volume (2/3 − (√3/4)·arccos(1/3))·π ≈ 0.419860 from the Reuleaux volume 0.422158.
Both Meissner bodies are compared with K (conjunction) to render 'the two Meissner tetrahedra'; they have equal volume, so this is equivalent to the single-inequality form in the decomposition note.

Extra declarations beyond the slot: `in_meissner_body.variants.unique_minimizers` (strong reading: the minimizers of volume among constant-width-w convex bodies are exactly the Meissner tetrahedra of width w, up to congruence, expressed via existence of a regular tetrahedron v with K = meissnerBodyVertex v w ∨ K = meissnerBodyFace v w), `hasConstantWidth_meissnerBody` (Meissner's classical theorem that the constructed bodies have constant width w, tagged research solved, sorry'd), and three proved `category test` API lemmas (closed ball has constant width 2r; Meissner bodies ⊆ Reuleaux tetrahedron; v 0 ∈ meissnerBodyVertex).
AMS tag 52 (convex and discrete geometry), matching the MSC of the primary literature (52A40, 52A15).

reviewer_notes: Statement ambiguity: the list entry's definite article admits a weaker (minimality) and a stronger (unique minimisers up to congruence) reading. The Wikipedia article and Bonnesen–Fenchel state minimality, so the slot declaration `in_meissner_body` uses the inequality reading; the stronger reading is shipped as a clearly labelled variant `in_meissner_body.variants.unique_minimizers` (a convex body of constant width w is a volume minimiser iff it equals a Meissner tetrahedron built on some regular tetrahedron of side w). Both noncongruent Meissner bodies are compared with K explicitly (they have equal volume, so this is equivalent to a single inequality). c07's missing-primitives bail-out ("no exact set-level construction available") is not persuasive: the Meissner bodies have a precise elementary description (Reuleaux tetrahedron with edge wedges replaced by spindles, or equivalently a ball polyhedron over three edge arcs), which five candidates formalised consistently and whose correctness I checked by hand (width formula, spindle geometry, wedge sector argument); three candidates independently reported numerical checks reproducing the known volume 0.41986 w³ and width 1. Final file = c05 with docstring polish only; compiles with only 'declaration uses sorry' warnings and passes `lake --wfail build` with the repository linters.
